screens.title: Operational Technology and Industrial Control Systems Security
screens.narratorSegment: Operational Technology and Industrial Control Systems are the systems that monitor and control physical processes. In practice this includes SCADA servers, PLCs, RTUs, distributed control systems, and the sensors and actuators they operate. In this lesson you will learn how OT differs from IT in priorities, lifespan, protocols, and operational constraints. That difference changes how we approach security: availability and safety often come first, patching is constrained, and specialized protocols are in use. You will also learn the Purdue Model, which provides a layered approach to segmenting OT networks, and specific controls such as industrial demilitarized zones, protocol-aware firewalls, anomaly detection, and careful change management. A concrete example you will see later is analyzing Modbus/TCP traffic to spot unauthorized write commands. Finally, we will cover common mistakes — like treating OT exactly like IT — and a practical safety note: any change to an active OT environment must be planned with OT engineers to avoid causing outages or physical harm. As you move through the module, ask how each control preserves availability and reduces risk to physical processes.

screens.title: IT vs OT: priorities and lifecycle contrast
screens.narratorSegment: Start by establishing the most important contrast: IT and OT have different primary goals. IT systems prioritize confidentiality and integrity of data; OT systems prioritize continuous operation and physical safety. This matters because a control that is sensible in IT can be dangerous in OT. For example, an IT-style automatic patch rollout that forces reboots could halt a production line or interfere with safety interlocks. Another difference is lifespan: OT assets may run for decades and use legacy operating systems without available patches. The practical consequence is that patching strategies must be risk-based and often rely on compensating controls like isolation. Connectivity also differs. OT was historically air-gapped, but modern requirements for telemetry and analytics have connected OT to IT, which creates new attack paths. Finally, OT uses specialized protocols such as Modbus/TCP and DNP3 that lack authentication in many deployments. Understanding these contrasts helps you design safer interventions: prefer segmentation, protocol-aware controls, and phased testing with OT teams. A common misconception is to treat OT as a copy of IT — that leads to outages. Your takeaway: always ask how an action affects physical safety and uptime before you apply it.

keyIdea.title: Why the difference matters
keyIdea.text: Security decisions must protect physical safety and availability; controls should be tested and sometimes compensated rather than blindly applied.

content.html:
Core Concept

IT vs OT

Compare priorities, lifespans, protocols, and connectivity so you can choose appropriate controls.
Priorities
IT: confidentiality first. OT: availability and safety first. This flips many risk decisions and affects incident response priorities.
Lifespan & Patching
OT equipment often runs for decades and cannot tolerate frequent reboots; patching is scheduled, prioritized, and sometimes impossible.
Protocols & Connectivity
OT uses Modbus, DNP3, OPC UA and similar protocols. Historically air-gapped, modern OT now often connects to IT for analytics, increasing attack surface.
Common Mistake

Treating OT like IT and applying automated patches or reboots without testing can cause outages or safety hazards.

Concrete example
Firmware patching on a PLC
A PLC firmware update requires a reboot and field recalibration. Applying it during operations could stop conveyors and trigger safety interlocks. The safer approach is lab testing, scheduled maintenance windows, and compensating isolation if patching is urgent.
Key Takeaway

Design controls that preserve uptime and safety; validate changes with OT engineers before applying them in production.

screens.title: What comprises OT and ICS
screens.narratorSegment: Operational Technology and Industrial Control Systems are a collection of hardware and software that monitor and control physical processes. SCADA is a supervisory architecture that provides high-level monitoring and control across geographically distributed sites. Distributed Control Systems are used within a plant to manage process control with tighter integration. PLCs—programmable logic controllers—are specialized industrial computers that run control logic and drive actuators. RTUs are remote terminal units that collect sensor input and relay it to central systems. Sensors and actuators are the field-level devices that sense conditions and perform physical actions. A concrete example: a water treatment plant uses sensors to measure flow and chemical levels, PLCs to control valves and pumps, and a SCADA server to display status and store logs. A common misconception is that ICS devices are simple; in reality they often run complex control sequences and must maintain precise timing and state. Understanding these components matters because each layer has different security and availability needs, and controls must be applied in ways that do not disturb control loops or safety interlocks. Keep in mind that many of these devices run legacy software, which affects how you approach updates and monitoring.

content.html:
Definition

OT and ICS Components

Recognize the role and constraints of SCADA, DCS, PLCs, RTUs, sensors, and actuators to apply appropriate security measures.

SCADA
Supervisory servers and GUIs that collect telemetry and coordinate control across sites.
DCS
Plant-level distributed control for continuous processes with real-time constraints.
PLC / RTU
Field controllers executing logic and connecting sensors and actuators to higher levels.
Concrete example
A water plant: sensors measure chlorine, PLCs set valve positions, SCADA logs events and alerts operators; a single malicious write to a PLC could open valves and cause overflow if not controlled.
Why it matters
Each device layer has different availability, timing, and update constraints, so security controls must be tailored and validated with OT teams.
Key Takeaway

Map OT components before applying controls; a correct inventory and an understanding of constraints prevents dangerous changes.

screens.title: Common OT attack vectors
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding common attack vectors helps you design defenses that prevent both access and dangerous commands. Many OT compromises begin with IT-to-OT convergence, where an attacker exploits a weak IT asset and pivots across the network. Remote access tools used for maintenance are another frequent route; if credentials are weak or MFA is absent, attackers gain powerful access. Removable media such as USB drives have historically delivered malware into isolated systems. Insider threats—both accidental and malicious—can alter configurations or introduce unsafe commands. Supply chain attacks can introduce vulnerabilities before systems are deployed. Finally, unauthenticated or unencrypted OT protocols permit attackers to send harmful function codes directly to controllers. A practical example: an attacker compromises a remote maintenance VPN account and issues unauthorized write commands to a PLC to change valve positions. A common misconception is that OT is safe because devices are specialized; in reality those specializations often include weak authentication. To prevent these threats, focus on segmentation, strict remote access controls, least-privilege accounts, vendor control processes, and protocol inspection to block malicious commands. Common OT attack vectors means pivoting from it, weak remote access, removable media, insiders, supply-chain, and vulnerable protocols are the main ways attackers reach ot.. In practical terms, how attackers reach and manipulate control systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Attack vector map
keyIdea.text: Pivoting from IT, weak remote access, removable media, insiders, supply-chain, and vulnerable protocols are the main ways attackers reach OT.

content.html:
Process Flow

Common OT attack vectors

1
IT-to-OT pivot
Compromise an IT asset and use network paths to reach OT devices that were never hardened for internet-exposed threats.
2
Remote access abuse
Vendor or maintenance remote access with weak authentication allows attackers to issue commands under an authorized session.
3
Removable media
USBs and laptops can introduce malware directly into isolated control networks during maintenance.
4
Insiders & supply chain
Insiders can make unsafe configuration changes. Supply-chain tampering can introduce compromised hardware or software at deployment.
Key Takeaway

Treat the IT-OT boundary as a focal defense point; protect remote access, control removable media, and validate supply-chain integrity.

Example scenario
An attacker steals credentials for a vendor remote-access account, logs into a maintenance VM, and issues Modbus write commands to a PLC to stop safety alarms. Detection was delayed because no protocol inspection was in place.
Prevention checklist
  • Segment IT and OT with an IDMZ
  • Use MFA and strictly log remote sessions
  • Enable protocol-aware IDS/IPS

screens.title: Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: The Purdue Model is a practical, hierarchical architecture for OT networks that divides systems into levels and enforces strict segmentation. The common levels run from Level 0 at process sensors and actuators, up through Level 1 for controllers like PLCs and RTUs, Level 2 for control workstations and HMIs, Level 3 for operations management and SCADA servers, an industrial DMZ between Levels 3 and 4, and Level 5 representing enterprise IT. The model's core principle is to minimize direct communication across levels and to allow only necessary, controlled flows—often exporting data upward but preventing downward control unless explicitly authorized. An Industrial DMZ or IDMZ is a buffer that mediates data between enterprise and control networks. Unidirectional gateways can enforce one-way flows where needed, ensuring that data can be collected without allowing commands to flow back. A concrete example: telemetry from Level 2 devices is sent to an analytics server in the IDMZ, but write access to Level 1 devices is blocked from the enterprise network. A common misconception is that the Purdue Model is a strict map to every site; in practice it is a guiding framework that must be adapted to each plant's topology and safety requirements. Your takeaway: use the Purdue Model to guide segmentation and enforce safe communication paths.

keyIdea.title: Segmentation principle
keyIdea.text: Use a layered model and IDMZs to control and limit communications between enterprise and control domains.

content.html:
Model

Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture

A layered approach that defines boundaries and controls communication between process, control, operations, and enterprise levels.

Level 0 - Process
Sensors and actuators that directly affect the world.
Level 1 - Basic Control
PLCs, RTUs, and controllers executing real-time logic.
Level 2-3 - HMI & Operations
HMIs, SCADA servers, and operations management systems.
IDMZ / Level 3.5
Buffer between enterprise IT and OT to control data flow.
Concrete configuration example
Place an industrial firewall and data historian in the IDMZ. Allow only selected telemetry to flow from Level 2 to the IDMZ, and block direct remote-write access from enterprise systems to Level 1 devices.
Key Takeaway

Adapt the Purdue Model to local topology; use the IDMZ to mediate and log all cross-domain communications.

screens.title: Network Segmentation and IDMZ
screens.narratorSegment: Network segmentation is the most critical control in OT security. By separating enterprise, operations, and control networks you reduce the risk that a compromised IT asset can reach a PLC or HMI. Segmentation is implemented through VLANs, industrial firewalls, and an IDMZ. The IDMZ acts as a controlled buffer: it receives telemetry and provides a minimal, well-audited set of services to the enterprise. A stronger option is a unidirectional gateway that physically enforces one-way data flow for telemetry when write access is not needed. When designing segmentation, evaluate allowed communication paths and explicitly deny everything else. Use industrial firewalls that understand Modbus and other OT protocols to apply application-layer rules rather than just port filters. A common misconception is to think segmentation is a one-time setup; it must be maintained with asset discovery and rule reviews. A concrete practice is to create service-level maps listing what servers need to talk to what devices and only permit those flows. Your takeaway: clear segmentation and an IDMZ reduce lateral movement and make detection and recovery far easier. Network Segmentation and IDMZ means enforce explicit allowlists, use protocol-aware controls, and consider unidirectional gateways for high-assurance telemetry.. In practical terms, how to separate duties and limit lateral movement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Best Practices

Network segmentation & IDMZ

Separate IT and OT, create an IDMZ, and enforce least-privilege communications using industrial-aware firewalls.

Allowlist communications
Explicitly list which servers may talk to which devices and drop everything else.
Protocol-aware firewalls
Use firewalls that inspect Modbus and other industrial protocols to block dangerous commands.
Unidirectional gateways
Where possible, enforce one-way telemetry flows to prevent command injection from enterprise networks.
Scenario
An enterprise analytics server requires telemetry but must not send commands. Placing it in the IDMZ with a unidirectional gateway lets analytics read data while guaranteeing no write path exists back to controllers.
Key Takeaway

Segment actively and review rules frequently; maintain service maps and restrict communication paths to the minimum required.

screens.title: Access control and vulnerability management
screens.narratorSegment: Access control and vulnerability management in OT must balance security with operational constraints. Start by implementing least-privilege access: accounts and service principals should have only the permissions they need to perform tasks. Remote access must use strong authentication and multi-factor authentication where feasible, and remote sessions should be logged and monitored. For vulnerability management, recognize that many OT devices cannot be patched quickly or at all. Instead of forcing immediate updates, prioritize assets by risk and adopt compensating controls such as network isolation, virtual patching with IPS, and enhanced monitoring for unpatchable systems. Always test patches in a lab that mirrors OT operations to ensure a patch won't disturb control loops or timing. A concrete example: identify a legacy PLC with a known vulnerability; if a vendor patch is unavailable, isolate the PLC with an industrial firewall, create strict allowlists, and place it under increased network and behavioral monitoring. A common misconception is that patching alone solves risk; in OT, a layered approach with compensating controls is often the safest route. The takeaway: combine least privilege, strong remote authentication, risk-based patching, and compensating isolation to protect OT assets without endangering availability.

keyIdea.title: Hardening approach
keyIdea.text: Use least privilege and risk-based patching with compensating controls when direct updates are impractical or risky.

content.html:
Control Set

Access & Vulnerability Management

Apply least privilege, strong authentication, and prioritize patching with compensating controls when needed.

Least privilege
Limit user and service rights to essential tasks and rotate credentials regularly.
Remote access controls
Use MFA, session logging, and vendor account governance to reduce risk from maintenance connections.
Compensating controls
Virtual patching, isolation, and monitoring protect unpatchable devices.
Example
A legacy PLC cannot be patched immediately. Isolate it behind an industrial firewall, allow only necessary management ports from a secured jump host, and enable enhanced anomaly logging to detect suspicious commands.
Pro Tip

Keep a staged test environment that mirrors OT timing and state so patches can be validated safely before production deployment.

screens.title: Protocol analysis and Modbus/TCP inspection
screens.narratorSegment: Protocol analysis is essential in OT because many industrial protocols lack strong authentication. When inspecting Modbus/TCP traffic, focus on fields like the transaction identifier, unit identifier, function code, reference number (address), and quantity or value. Function codes matter because they indicate read or write intent; unusual write function codes or unexpected addresses often indicate malicious activity. A concrete exercise is to open a PCAP in Wireshark, filter for Modbus traffic, expand the Modbus/TCP layer, and inspect function codes such as Read Holding Registers and Write Single Coil. In practice look for patterns like write commands outside maintenance windows, unusual unit identifiers, or transactions that write to safety-critical addresses. A common misconception is that signature-based IDS alone will catch these issues; signatures often miss novel or subtle manipulation. Behavioral analysis—spotting anomalous sequences or out-of-schedule writes—is more effective. When you analyze packets, document the session identifiers and timestamps so you can correlate with operational logs and control-room events. Your takeaway: focus on function codes and addresses, correlate with operations context, and favor anomaly-based detection when signatures are insufficient. Protocol analysis and Modbus/TCP inspection means watch function codes, addresses, and timing; anomalous writes to control registers are strong indicators of compromise.. In practical terms, what to look for when analyzing industrial traffic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Anomaly detection for OT
screens.narratorSegment: Anomaly detection is particularly valuable in OT where signature-based systems may miss novel commands or protocol misuse. Behavior-based systems learn normal patterns—such as command timing, typical function codes, and usual unit identifiers—and alert on deviations like unusual write frequency or out-of-hours control commands. Start by establishing baselines for device behavior and scheduled maintenance windows. Use network flow and protocol-aware telemetry to feed anomaly models. A concrete example: if a PLC typically receives one status request every five minutes but suddenly receives multiple write commands at odd hours, that triggers an alert and an operator investigation. Misconceptions include over-reliance on anomaly systems without tuning; false positives are common if models are not trained with representative operational data. To reduce noise, combine rule-based filtering (deny unknown unit IDs) with anomaly detection and prioritize alerts that target safety-critical addresses. Always integrate alerts with an operational incident workflow so that safety experts can quickly decide containment steps. Your takeaway: use anomaly detection as a core control, but tune models with real operational data and pair them with procedural response plans. Detection

Anomaly detection in OT

How it works
  • Collect normal traffic patterns and device command rates.
  • Train models on periodicity, command types, and authorized unit IDs.
  • Alert on deviations such as unexpected writes, timing anomalies, or new endpoints.
Example
A PLC that normally receives telemetry polls suddenly receives multiple write requests outside maintenance hours—anomaly detection raises a high-priority alert for investigation.
Reduce false positives
Train with representative data, exclude known maintenance windows, and correlate with operational logs before escalating.
Key Takeaway

Anomaly detection catches novel attacks, but only when tuned and paired with operational response procedures.

screens.title: Incident response and safety-first planning
screens.narratorSegment: Incident response in OT must put safety and availability first. An OT-specific IR plan defines roles, communication paths, containment steps that do not endanger processes, and restoration procedures. Before an incident, perform tabletop exercises that include OT engineers, operations staff, and safety officers. During an incident, containment may mean isolating a segment, disabling specific remote connections, or switching to manual control modes rather than shutting systems down abruptly. Recovery emphasizes restoring operational capability quickly: bring systems back in a controlled sequence and verify safety interlocks before resuming full operations. Backup and recovery strategies should include configuration backups for PLCs, verified images for control servers, and procedures to restore stateful control parameters. A common pitfall is to run an IT-style forensics process that takes devices offline; in OT this can be hazardous. Instead, collect evidence passively where possible and consult OT personnel before making changes. Your takeaway: prepare IR playbooks that balance evidence collection with immediate steps to maintain safety and production. Engage OT teams early and test your plans regularly. OT Incident Response

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety considerations
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring mistakes that undermine OT security and can cause real-world harm. Treating OT identically to IT is a top error: automated reboots, broad scans, or untested configuration changes can interrupt control loops and trigger safety events. Connecting OT devices directly to the internet without an IDMZ or industrial firewall exposes critical controllers to remote attacks. Using default credentials or weak vendor accounts is another frequent issue—these easily enable attackers to operate devices. Additionally, failing to involve OT engineers in security changes risks unintended consequences. Always plan changes with OT staff, validate them in a lab, and schedule maintenance windows. Physical security is equally critical: control rooms and key devices must be physically protected to prevent tampering. Finally, document and rehearse recovery procedures. A concrete example: running an aggressive vulnerability scanner against a control network caused a PLC to drop communications with an HMI, creating a temporary loss of situational awareness. The correct approach is targeted, non-intrusive scanning and coordination. Your takeaway: prioritize safety in every security action and avoid shortcuts that jeopardize operations. Safety Note

Common mistakes that cause harm

Treating OT like IT
Applying automated patches, scans, or reboots without testing can stop production or disable safety systems.
Direct internet exposure
Placing controllers online without an IDMZ invites remote attackers into control spaces.
Weak credentials & vendor access
Default or unmanaged vendor accounts are a common entry point for attackers.
Real incident

An intrusive scan caused a PLC to lose HMI communication. The plant lost temporary visibility, illustrating why non-intrusive methods and coordination are essential.

Key Takeaway

Always validate security actions in a lab, involve OT engineers, and protect physical access to control equipment.

fullNarratorScript:
Operational Technology and Industrial Control Systems are the systems that monitor and control physical processes. In practice this includes SCADA servers, PLCs, RTUs, distributed control systems, and the sensors and actuators they operate. In this lesson you will learn how OT differs from IT in priorities, lifespan, protocols, and operational constraints. That difference changes how we approach security: availability and safety often come first, patching is constrained, and specialized protocols are in use. You will also learn the Purdue Model, which provides a layered approach to segmenting OT networks, and specific controls such as industrial demilitarized zones, protocol-aware firewalls, anomaly detection, and careful change management. A concrete example you will see later is analyzing Modbus/TCP traffic to spot unauthorized write commands. Finally, we will cover common mistakes — like treating OT exactly like IT — and a practical safety note: any change to an active OT environment must be planned with OT engineers to avoid causing outages or physical harm. As you move through the module, ask how each control preserves availability and reduces risk to physical processes.

Over this chapter you will develop five practical skills that reflect the realities of operational environments. First, you will be able to distinguish IT from OT and describe why availability and safety take precedence in OT. This matters because it changes how you prioritize controls and respond to incidents. Second, you'll identify common attack vectors in OT environments, such as IT-to-OT pivoting, remote access compromise, and vulnerable protocols. Knowing these vectors lets you design defenses targeted to real threats. Third, you will be able to explain the Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture and use it to propose segmentation and IDMZ strategies. Fourth, you will learn practical OT controls: industrial firewalls, strict access control, tailored vulnerability management, and anomaly detection. Each control will be tied to safety and uptime. Finally, you will practice protocol analysis and traffic inspection using the Modbus/TCP example, learning how to spot malicious function codes. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual to help you remember the goal and a verified competency milestone so you can check your mastery.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical analysis and incident preparedness. You will practice protocol analysis for Modbus, DNP3, and OPC UA, learning which fields to inspect and how malicious function codes can change actuator states. This is important because attackers often exploit unauthenticated protocol fields to cause physical effects. You will also learn to plan OT incident response: how to prioritize safety, coordinate with plant engineers, and restore operations quickly. Finally, you will be prepared to design vulnerability management that accepts constraints—where patching is limited—and to use compensating controls like isolation and intrusion prevention. Each objective ties to a short milestone you can test in lab or tabletop exercises, and each includes a mnemonic or simple diagram to help you remember the steps. These skills make you able to detect, isolate, and respond to OT threats while preserving critical uptime and safety.

Start by establishing the most important contrast: IT and OT have different primary goals. IT systems prioritize confidentiality and integrity of data; OT systems prioritize continuous operation and physical safety. This matters because a control that is sensible in IT can be dangerous in OT. For example, an IT-style automatic patch rollout that forces reboots could halt a production line or interfere with safety interlocks. Another difference is lifespan: OT assets may run for decades and use legacy operating systems without available patches. The practical consequence is that patching strategies must be risk-based and often rely on compensating controls like isolation. Connectivity also differs. OT was historically air-gapped, but modern requirements for telemetry and analytics have connected OT to IT, which creates new attack paths. Finally, OT uses specialized protocols such as Modbus/TCP and DNP3 that lack authentication in many deployments. Understanding these contrasts helps you design safer interventions: prefer segmentation, protocol-aware controls, and phased testing with OT teams. A common misconception is to treat OT as a copy of IT — that leads to outages. Your takeaway: always ask how an action affects physical safety and uptime before you apply it.

Operational Technology and Industrial Control Systems are a collection of hardware and software that monitor and control physical processes. SCADA is a supervisory architecture that provides high-level monitoring and control across geographically distributed sites. Distributed Control Systems are used within a plant to manage process control with tighter integration. PLCs—programmable logic controllers—are specialized industrial computers that run control logic and drive actuators. RTUs are remote terminal units that collect sensor input and relay it to central systems. Sensors and actuators are the field-level devices that sense conditions and perform physical actions. A concrete example: a water treatment plant uses sensors to measure flow and chemical levels, PLCs to control valves and pumps, and a SCADA server to display status and store logs. A common misconception is that ICS devices are simple; in reality they often run complex control sequences and must maintain precise timing and state. Understanding these components matters because each layer has different security and availability needs, and controls must be applied in ways that do not disturb control loops or safety interlocks. Keep in mind that many of these devices run legacy software, which affects how you approach updates and monitoring.

Understanding common attack vectors helps you design defenses that prevent both access and dangerous commands. Many OT compromises begin with IT-to-OT convergence, where an attacker exploits a weak IT asset and pivots across the network. Remote access tools used for maintenance are another frequent route; if credentials are weak or MFA is absent, attackers gain powerful access. Removable media such as USB drives have historically delivered malware into isolated systems. Insider threats—both accidental and malicious—can alter configurations or introduce unsafe commands. Supply chain attacks can introduce vulnerabilities before systems are deployed. Finally, unauthenticated or unencrypted OT protocols permit attackers to send harmful function codes directly to controllers. A practical example: an attacker compromises a remote maintenance VPN account and issues unauthorized write commands to a PLC to change valve positions. A common misconception is that OT is safe because devices are specialized; in reality those specializations often include weak authentication. To prevent these threats, focus on segmentation, strict remote access controls, least-privilege accounts, vendor control processes, and protocol inspection to block malicious commands. The Purdue Model is a practical, hierarchical architecture for OT networks that divides systems into levels and enforces strict segmentation. The common levels run from Level 0 at process sensors and actuators, up through Level 1 for controllers like PLCs and RTUs, Level 2 for control workstations and HMIs, Level 3 for operations management and SCADA servers, an industrial DMZ between Levels 3 and 4, and Level 5 representing enterprise IT. The model's core principle is to minimize direct communication across levels and to allow only necessary, controlled flows—often exporting data upward but preventing downward control unless explicitly authorized. An Industrial DMZ or IDMZ is a buffer that mediates data between enterprise and control networks. Unidirectional gateways can enforce one-way flows where needed, ensuring that data can be collected without allowing commands to flow back. A concrete example: telemetry from Level 2 devices is sent to an analytics server in the IDMZ, but write access to Level 1 devices is blocked from the enterprise network. A common misconception is that the Purdue Model is a strict map to every site; in practice it is a guiding framework that must be adapted to each plant's topology and safety requirements. Your takeaway: use the Purdue Model to guide segmentation and enforce safe communication paths.

Network segmentation is the most critical control in OT security. By separating enterprise, operations, and control networks you reduce the risk that a compromised IT asset can reach a PLC or HMI. Segmentation is implemented through VLANs, industrial firewalls, and an IDMZ. The IDMZ acts as a controlled buffer: it receives telemetry and provides a minimal, well-audited set of services to the enterprise. A stronger option is a unidirectional gateway that physically enforces one-way data flow for telemetry when write access is not needed. When designing segmentation, evaluate allowed communication paths and explicitly deny everything else. Use industrial firewalls that understand Modbus and other OT protocols to apply application-layer rules rather than just port filters. A common misconception is to think segmentation is a one-time setup; it must be maintained with asset discovery and rule reviews. A concrete practice is to create service-level maps listing what servers need to talk to what devices and only permit those flows. Your takeaway: clear segmentation and an IDMZ reduce lateral movement and make detection and recovery far easier.
